text: Some summers change football. This is the album of one of them.
In the summer of nineteen seventy-four, three men from FC Barcelona went to the World Cup in West Germany wearing orange.
Barça's coach, Rinus Michels. Barça's star, Johan Cruyff. And a midfielder who would sign for Barça the moment it was over — Johan Neeskens.
Six weeks, seven matches, one final. Let's open the album, page by page.
And remember this picture. It's from the match where Cruyff invented a move that still carries his name.
Page one. The champions arrive.
In April, Barcelona had become Spanish champions for the first time in fourteen years. A month later, they were still touring — here, in the Netherlands, against PSV.
Cruyff was the reason Barça had won. He had arrived the summer before, for a world-record fee.
At the Dutch training camp in Zeist, he met up with an old team-mate from Ajax: Johan Neeskens.
And the national team was handed to Barça's coach. Rinus Michels would lead the Netherlands while still working for Barcelona.
Page two. The camp.
The Dutch squad set up camp at a hotel in Hiltrup, near Münster. Crowds were waiting for them the moment they arrived.
Every window, every training session, every interview was news.
Wives and families visited. Photographers climbed fences to get a picture.
And in the middle of it all, Michels — the General — tried to keep his players focused on football.
Page three. The group.
The first game was against Uruguay in Hanover. Johnny Rep scored twice. Two–nil.

Then came Sweden, in Dortmund. Nil–nil. But in that match Cruyff did something that still has a name today. With the ball at his feet and a defender in front of him, he faked a pass — and dragged the ball back behind his standing leg, turning away in one movement. The defender was left behind. People call it the Cruyff turn.
Outside, Dutch supporters were having their own tournament — some of them in the fountains.
Against Bulgaria, the Netherlands won four–one. Neeskens scored twice from the penalty spot. The orange team was through.
Page four. The masterclass.
In the second round, the Netherlands destroyed Argentina four–nil in the rain in Gelsenkirchen. Cruyff scored twice.
Then East Germany, two–nil — Neeskens and Rob Rensenbrink.
And then the reigning world champions, Brazil. Neeskens scored with a delicate chip, and Cruyff volleyed in the second. Two–nil. The Netherlands were in the final.
It was a brutal game. At one point Neeskens was kicked so hard he lay unconscious on the grass. He got up and finished the match.
Page five. The final.
Seventh of July, Munich's Olympic Stadium. The hosts, West Germany, led by Franz Beckenbauer. Cruyff and Beckenbauer exchanged pennants before kick-off.

From the kick-off, the Dutch passed the ball between them more than a dozen times. Then Cruyff ran into the box and was brought down. Neeskens hit the penalty straight down the middle. One–nil, before a German player had touched the ball.
But West Germany equalised with a penalty of their own, from Paul Breitner, and then Gerd Müller turned and scored just before half-time.
In the second half, the Dutch attacked and attacked. It stayed two–one. The best team of the tournament had lost the final.
Page six. Back to Barcelona.
The next day, thousands of people filled the streets of Amsterdam to welcome the team home. They hadn't won — but nobody seemed to care.
Eleven days after the final, Neeskens and his new wife flew to Barcelona. Michels and Cruyff were already there, getting ready for a new season.
In November, Cruyff received a golden ball as the best player of the World Cup.

And the ideas the world had seen that summer — pressing, moving, everyone attacking and everyone defending — went back to Barcelona with them. Fourteen years later, Cruyff would return to build an entire club on them.
They lost the final. But in a way, they won something bigger: the future of how football would be played.
Is the Netherlands of nineteen seventy-four the best team never to win the World Cup? Tell me in the comments.
